body:
“The Last House,” a science-fiction horror from French director Louis Leterrier, is a movie born from Covid.

	A suburban family of four, helmed by Jason (Wagner Moura) and Ann (Greta Lee), is suddenly trapped in their home. With no understanding of the situation outside, and no way to know how long it will last, they must adjust to life inside.

	Matthew Robinson wrote the first act during the pandemic, but when Leterrier read it, he thought there was something more to the story. “Let’s use the global experience and understanding that the pandemic brought on people, which is how we survived physically at first, but then most importantly, ours is how we survive psychologically, emotionally afterward,” he says.
	

	The “something more,” as the family comes to realize, is the mysterious presence sealing them inside their house. As the days stretch on, they must work together to survive — physically, mentally, emotionally.


	Ahead of the film’s release Aug. 7 on Netflix, Leterrier and Moura sat down with Variety to talk about the inspiration behind “The Last House,” the parenting perspective they brought to the project and the physical and emotional experience of shooting.
	
		We see someone die pretty early in the movie. How did you approach these characters who experience those kinds of things really quickly, and then we have a lot of time left in the movie to play with?	

	Louis Leterrier: We had one breakfast, one happy breakfast, and then bam.

	Wagner Moura: I read the script, and the Covid thing was for sure something that resonated real fast with me, because my experience with Covid was the idea of an external threat. In Brazil, it was a tragedy. So many people died. At the same time, I was experiencing something very unique with my family at home. I had never stayed so long with them and really had the time to be with them, look at each one of my sons, my wife. I had a very intimate moment with them, beautiful moments, intense moments. Then it was the Louis factor because I had this breakfast with him, and was like, ‘I want to work with this dude.’ I had an immediate connection with him. Also, I had never done anything like this before. For me, this is about a family, but it’s also a family movie that resembles those films that I grew up watching, from the ‘80s and ‘90s. It was a no-brainer for me.
	

	Leterrier: Wagner knows, but one day I was in line for sushi, a gimmicky sushi restaurant next to where Wagner lives, where robots serve you sushi and drinks. And I saw him, and I was super starstruck. My wife was like, ‘You’re weird,’ because I know everyone in Hollywood, but I’d never met Wagner, and he’s so amazing in his movies. I was like, ‘Do you want to go have breakfast with me?’ And we talked about the movie in general, we talked about each other and we talked about life.
	
		On that note of it being a family movie, I was really struck by a lot of moments where Jason and Ann are trying to decide if they’re going to tell their kids the full truth or not. How did you decide which things were going to be the full truth for those kids, and which were going to be kept secret from them?	

	Leterrier: It’s what you do as a parent. You guide your family toward your version, what you think is the right version of the world, and you try to protect them from the ugly truth. Sometimes the painful truth. But you don’t try to create a bubble for them. Although Jason and Ann, Greta’s character, are trying to build a bubble in the beginning. In Covid, there was the same thing. We didn’t know how long Covid would last, so that was the instinct in the beginning. There are levels of opening up and telling the truth, and at one point you just can’t hide it because your kids are so instinctive. They can see when there’s a problem with their parents.

	Moura: It’s a difficult balance. One thing that really connected us, Louis and Greta and I, is the fact that we are all parents, and we understand what it is when your kid is sick, or I can’t even imagine having a kid that’s starving or anything like that. We would do anything for them, and one of the things is protecting them. Jason, he’s so focused on taking care of his kids. He’s a man that, at some point, he’s so focused on doing what he thinks is his job, to protect them, that he forgets about them. This is something that happens sometimes. I sometimes forget to listen to my kids, especially when they’re little, because parents, we have this arrogance, or adults in general, that we know the truth and we know everything. His daughter is telling him something since the beginning of the film, and he just doesn’t listen to her. Another thing that I realized is that in order to take care of someone, you need to allow other people to take care of you, and that’s the point where Jason breaks. It’s that he never allowed anyone to take care of him as well. There are so many different layers of what to be a parent is, or to be an adult in the world is, that I think this film brings.
	

	Leterrier: It’s a very personal movie for all of us. That’s the way I feel about the world — maybe Wagner feels the same way — Jason’s starting point of not being able to control the world outside or being so lost with the situation. And when this happens, you’re able to grab the reins of the situation and then say, ‘OK, that’s the world. I’m able to do this.’ But then, by doing so, you go a little too deep. And as Wagner was saying, Jason loses himself and becomes blind. He becomes obsessed about one thing: feeding his family, survival.
	
		I want to talk about that scene where Jason does lose it in the garage. That was one of the most striking scenes for me throughout the film.	

	Moura: No one is that tough. No one can carry the weight of the world on their shoulders. There are moments where Ann is trying to tell him, ‘Look at us. We’re here.’ And especially his daughter is trying to tell him something, and he just doesn’t listen. It’s only natural for me that he would break at some point. That was a very strong scene. Louis and I spoke about losing your ability to take care of yourself psychologically. At some point, I think the audience goes, ‘This dude is losing his mind.’ He’s breaking not only psycho-emotionally, but he’s going nuts. This film was unexpectedly hard to shoot physically. None of us expected this to be that. This scene, driving the car, crashing the car, coming back. We did it so many (times). But not only that, I wasn’t expecting this to be so — I’m not even mentioning the water part of it all — but it was very physically demanding. But it was physically demanding because it was also emotionally demanding.

	Leterrier: You and Greta were so committed. There was some incredible weight loss, gaining weight again, losing weight again, getting old on camera. It was like stripping at the end. If I turned the camera on the crew, you would have seen the same effect. This movie was so hard because we didn’t make it easy. Sorry, my fault. I didn’t make it easy on any of you guys because I wanted everything to be real. Practical, practical, practical. The grass was real. The plants they grew were real. We worked backward, so we had to know what the house looked like at the end and then build on top of it. The animals were 100% real. They were biting. They were mean. George, that squirrel, is really not a nice actor. He’s the worst actor you have ever worked with. Wagner, you and Greta were so committed to this movie. It would have been easy to come in and out, go to your luxurious hotel room, come back and everything. We were like, ‘We’re focused on this movie. We’re staying in this movie, we’re staying in character.’ There’s only so much I can do as a director. I can brief Wagner and Greta, but when we start rolling, he has to interact with kids who are not actors, animals, rain, special effects. I’m throwing a lot of stuff in the air, and then Greta and Wagner are dealing with it and doing so well. So much of acting is reacting. There’s this real truth captured on camera on this one.
	
	
		What’s next for you both after this?	

	Moura: Right now, I’m touring with my play here in Europe, which has been great. It’s a play called “A Trial — after An Enemy of the People.” It’s a play on (Henrik) Ibsen’s play (“An Enemy of the People”). This has been so great too, because this is happening throughout the entire summer, and I’m having my family here with me. It’s been so many different countries. And right after this, I’m shooting the “Oceans” film, which I’m very excited about. And then I’m gonna direct my film. Louis, did I tell you this?

	Leterrier: Oh, amazing! “Last Night at the Lobster.” Amazing. Love this movie.

	Moura: Finally financed. So, this is gonna be my year.

	Leterrier: That’s how we met. We were talking about this movie, and we nerded out on this. I’m finishing a movie called “Liminal” with Vanessa Kirby, Yahya Abdul-Mateen, Tom Pelphrey, Tracy Letts, Paul Sparks, lots of kids too. It’s pretty amazing. Franka Potente, amazing actress. It’s a big sci-fi movie shot in New York. I don’t make it easy on myself. I always choose the difficult ones, it seems. Most importantly, I want to hang out with Wagner.

	Moura: I want to hang out with Louis, too. He’s coming to France, and we’re gonna have some nice French wine and talk about the next project together.

	Leterrier: While reading Variety.

	Watch an exclusive “Last House” featurette below.

title: Jean Grey Speaks: Sadie Sink on Making Her MCU Debut in ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ and the Mutant’s Future With the New X-Men

body:
SPOILER ALERT: This interview contains spoilers for, including the ending of, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” now playing in theaters.

	For more than a year, Sadie Sink had to keep her role in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” a secret. Sink, who was offered the part after her breakout performances in “Stranger Things” and “The Whale,” showed up to the London set without having read a full script. For security, her character was referred to with a code name.

	When it came time to promote the film this summer, the trailers hadn’t revealed more than the fact that Sink’s character is a hooded figure with questionable intentions — and the ability to jump into anyone’s mind. So, even as Sink showed up for photo calls with her co-stars Tom Holland and Zendaya and partook in interviews, she had to find creative ways to talk around what she’d done on set.

	As obvious as it might’ve been to the Marvel faithful that Sink was playing Jean Grey, the Omega-level mutant who will go on to star in the studio’s upcoming “X-Men” movie, Sink wasn’t going to be the one who spoiled it.

	And she didn’t. Steve Lacy did — right at the finish line.

	At the film’s world premiere in Los Angeles, the R&B singer, who has a song on the “Brand New Day” soundtrack, revealed that his favorite character from the movie was the villain, “Jean,” during the official red carpet live stream. “She’s the villain but, like, there’s a reason to her madness,” he said.

	What did Sink make of that moment? “Honestly, it was amazing!” Sink tells Variety, laughing. “I was like, ‘Ah!’ He kind of set me free in a lot of ways. And I’m such a big fan of his.”

	To be fair, Sink had already told a few trusted people the truth, including her “Stranger Things” bosses, Matt and Ross Duffer. But now that the movie is in theaters (supplanting “Avengers: Endgame” as the biggest domestic debut in box office history and grossing $1.15 billion worldwide in just seven days) and Sink’s secret identity is revealed, she’s finally gotten the green light to discuss her experience as the third actress to play the role after Famke Janssen in Fox’s “X-Men” movies and Sophie Turner in the 2010s reboot movies.

	In her first interview since “Brand New Day” debuted, Sink explains how she got cast in the role, how she developed her take on the character and her excitement about what’s to come when Jean joins the X-Men. The one thing Sink can’t reveal is how many Marvel movies she’s signed on for.

	“I can’t really say …” Sink demurs when asked if her contract runs two movies or 10. (Kevin Feige is always watching.)

	Read on for more. 
	
		Congratulations! You can finally talk about it.	

	I know, what a relief.
	
		What’s one question you’ve been dying to answer?	

	I don’t know. I haven’t even thought about it. I’ve mostly just been thinking about what I can’t say. So now that I can say stuff, I’m like, ‘Wait, how do I talk about this?’


	
		Where would you like to start with Jean? Because this is a character that people love from the comics and from the other movies. How big a fan were you before this opportunity came?	

	Honestly, I knew nothing about her. People had started rumors about me playing that character — for like years, it had kind of been circulating online — so that was all I knew about her. But I had never seen “X-Men,” so I was just like unfamiliar.

	Then Kevin [Feige] and Louis [D’Esposito] from Marvel called me, set up a meeting, and just told me about the character, about her role in “Spider-Man.” Then I did more research on her, and I was like, “Oh yeah, this is a no-brainer!” She’s such an iconic figure in X-Men and in comics, and I’m very excited to bring my iteration of her to life.



	
		This version of Jean Grey is different from what we’ve seen in other movies. For one, it explores her relationship with her sister, Sara. What interested you about that part of the story?	

	Giving [Jean] a backstory is really important — especially given her actions in the film. She’s very flawed. You’re meeting her at a strange point, because I don’t think she is someone who wants to harm, but she herself has been harmed, so that’s all she knows. So, giving her that backstory and a motive behind her actions is really powerful.

	They told me that I was the villain, but that you’re not actually the villain, which is how I played her. I don’t really want to lean into, like this bad guy aura. Because in her brain it’s totally justified. Which I mean, I agree. I think it is.




	

					Sadie Sink at the photo call for “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” in New York.
									Christopher Polk/@polkimaging
	




	
		Well, yes. When you read in the script what V-Max actually stands for, what was your reaction? Because people gasped in the theater.	

	Well, at first, I was like, “Is the sister in the vent?” [Laughs.] Then I kept on reading the script, and I was like, “Oh my god, wait, that’s so much better that it means absolutely nothing.”

	I remember in the original script there was more dialogue surrounding the realization that it meant nothing. Jean had lines where she was talking it out loud. Then, on the day, it was kind of like, “Oh no, I think it just needs to be a look.” It’s gonna be clearer, like you don’t really need to speak it through. I like that that’s the thing that unleashes her, just that anger over all of it being for nothing.

	I think, also, she kind of knew that her sister was gone. She’s been hanging on to this last piece of information, but I think she knows that it’s a long shot that she’s even still around. So, it was just kind of like the final trigger for her or the final confirmation.


	
		She was holding on to hope that she would see her sister again, and then to get confirmed that no, this is where my sister died is a pretty brutal realization. Did you take Sara’s scrunchie from set?	

	I did not take that. I took the jumpsuit she wears, just because I thought it was really comfortable. I haven’t worn it yet, and now I probably can’t because that would be a little bit cringy, I think. But it really is like a super comfortable jumpsuit. There was also a suede jacket, like the Penny Lane jacket [from “Almost Famous”]. I tried that on in a fitting, and I was kind of obsessed with the idea of it, but we never actually used it, and I asked, “Can I keep it?” That was all I took.
	
		Maybe you can take it with you to the next movie?	

	Hopefully. Yeah, we’ve got to get it in somehow.



	
		Coincidentally, some of the biggest searches for your name and Jean are for “wig” and “costume.” What is it like to know that Jean’s going to be a Halloween costume again, much like Max was for “Stranger Things?”	

	I didn’t even think about that, but I hope to see a lot of Jean Greys. That would be cool. It’s a super easy one to recreate.
	
		The costume itself is easy, but all the work that you did was tricky. One of my colleagues wondered how your neck is doing between “Stranger Things” and thrashing around when Jean’s being experimented on in “Brand New Day?”	

	Oh my god! Thank you so much for asking. Now that I’m thinking about it, I feel like I spent a week in that chair, like shooting all those [scenes], because we had to get so much coverage. So, I spent a long time in the chair, and my neck, yeah, I was definitely feeling it. When you’re watching it, it goes by in a second, but no, you’re there all day, just thrashing around.


	But I always like those physical things as an actor. If you’re working through something or like doing something with your body, it connects you more to the emotion.


	
		There was so much secrecy around this role. Who were the three people that you told you got the part?	

	I mean, it was definitely more than three, if I’m being honest. You have people that you can trust within the industry to talk about it. So, my family knew and everything, and then I slowly … like the Duffers were some of the first few people I told. Because I was filming with them, and they’re obviously huge influences in my career and life, and have watched me grow up, so I wanted them to know that that’s what I would be doing next. And they were so excited.
	
		Did they have any thoughts or advice?	

	Well, they were just like, “That’s the best character. You have to do it!” and like, “That’s perfect. You’re going to be amazing,” and blah blah blah. They thought it was the right fit for me, and I trust their opinion because they love comics and stuff like that, and are very well versed with these characters, so it was good to have their input.
	
		Did anyone else from “Stranger Things” find out before they got to the theater?	

	I didn’t really tell anybody else. That was kind of it.

	
		Did your character really have a code name in the script? Jacob Batalon joked that it was “Denim Red,” but is that true?	

	It definitely wasn’t “Denim Red.” There was a code name, but I can’t remember. “Denim Red” is cooler than whatever it was.





	

					“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” director Destin Daniel Cretton, center, with stars Michael Mando, Liza Colón-Zayas, Sadie Sink, Jon Bernthal, Tom Holland, Tramell Tillman, Zendaya, Marvin Jones III, Jacob Batalon and Eman Esfandi at the world premiere in Los Angeles.
									Sony Pictures via Getty Images
	



	
		Just like you’d grown up with the Duffers, you’d already worked with Destin on “The Glass Castle.” What excited you about reuniting with him?	

	Well, it’s overwhelming joining these huge franchises. I was in a similar position with “Stranger Things” — but even that feels smaller than entering the Spider-Man/Marvel world — joining in season two as a new kid. It felt similar to that, except Destin was involved. I have the best memories of doing that first movie with him because I hadn’t spent much time on set — I was a theater kid — so I really learned a lot from that summer that we worked on “Glass Castle.” He’s such a good guy, such a comforting presence. He really keeps his family close, and he’s just got great values and brings that to set. So, it was nice to have a familiar face and someone you trust. And the whole [“Spider-Man”] group was incredible and couldn’t have been lovelier, but it was nice to know going into it that you have a connection. That it’s not just a total group of strangers.


	
		Destin has said that he asked Marvel and Kevin Feige to include Jean Grey; it was not a mandate. But he wanted the character for a specific reason. In those early conversations, what did he tell you about his plans that helped you prep?	

	In the early conversations and rehearsals, it was always just really important to him that she’s a young girl in pain. In finding her voice and figuring out what it would look like, there is this pressure to live up to what a villain in a superhero movie looks like, but our plan was to just go the opposite way. To not focus on the evil bits and play into that too much, but rather the really angry, hurt teenager — which I have experience in playing, it seems. [Laughs.]


	
		Tell me about the hurt. One of the most poignant scenes in the movie is when Peter finally lets Jean into his mind, and she has this conversation with Aunt May, who tells her, “The people who love you, we love you not because you’re special, we love you because you’re you.” Tell me about shooting that scene with Marisa Tomei and Tom Holland.	

	I was so excited to get to that scene just because it feels like every scene before that is her suppressing emotion or hurt, and dealing with it through her powers or through manipulating others. But that’s kind of when the walls come down when she just hears everything that she needs to hear in that moment. Because as strong as she seems and as her actions are, she’s really just so terrified and so alone, and I think resents Peter up until that point for thinking that he’s not alone.

	Like the whole thing with MJ too, it’s like, well, “You’re holding on to the memory of having people in your life, but they’re gone, and you don’t get to have that.” That’s what the whole MJ manipulation was for: to remind him that like, “Oh yeah, this is what you can’t have, and this is what this has taken from you.”

	So, I guess in that final moment, she’s backed into a corner where it’s like, “Yeah, this person has hurt too,” but what he’s done with his loss and isolation, he’s turned it around and is offering her what he’s learned. And it’s kind of what he needs to hear and remind himself of in that moment, too.So yeah, shooting that was nice, and I had like a good idea of like what needed to be done. I think that was my last day of shooting too, so it just felt like a perfect way to just tie it up and show the core of who she is in that moment.




	

					Sadie Sink as Jean Grey in “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”
									Jay Maidment/Sony
	



	
		You mentioned the manipulation — when did you see how your co-stars changed their performances when Jean was mind-controlling them?	

	Tom and I did rehearsals, and then we had a full day where we shot every single scene where I’m talking through someone else — we have that on camera, somewhere — as a reference to send to all of the actors who had a line. It was cool; you can kind of see how people are like carrying it or mimicking me in certain ways — Zendaya, especially. I hadn’t seen her scene until I watched it for the first time, and it’s so cool to see that.
	
		Was the first time at the L.A. premiere?	

	No, I had seen it before, just by myself in a screening room.
	
		What was that like?	

	It was fun. I had no idea what to expect. But that was the interesting part too, because I really only worked like 20 days on the film. Most of the work was done in preproduction, or I would come in for certain days to block scenes; even if I wasn’t in it, I’d be there to have some say in the physicality of it. But there was so much of the movie that I hadn’t seen, so it was so cool to watch as a fan to see all the other aspects.


	
		In Jean’s final scene, is she heading upstate to Westchester, where the X Mansion is?	

	Oh, I don’t really know yet, to be honest. And when I say “I don’t know,” I mean I really don’t know. [Laughs.]


	
		What conversations have you had with Jake Schreier about where he wants to take the character? Because we do know that Jean will return in “X-Men.”	

	Yes, she will. It’s been really exciting all the conversations we’ve had, and I feel really lucky that I have this introduction through “Spider-Man” and [her] backstory. I think that’s what X-Men is all about, too. The more I’ve gotten into it and researched, what makes them special is that they are all incredibly flawed and maybe have done bad things. That makes them more compelling, complex characters and a more complex hero if they don’t start out that way. And they have to find their relationship to their powers. Because it’s not like they’ve asked for this or that these strengths make their lives easier; they make them a lot harder, actually. So, knowing Jean’s struggle will be important in the future of her character and where she goes, just makes her really well-rounded, which I’m excited for.


	
		Have you gotten a chance to meet any of your rumored castmates? We heard earlier today that Kit Connor is likely going to join you as Scott Summers/Cyclops and Samara Weaving as Emma Frost.	

	I have not, but I hope to very soon. I love the idea that it’s going to be a really awesome ensemble. I can’t wait. I’m getting super, super pumped about it.



	

					Sadie Sink poses with fans at the world premiere of “Spider-Man: Brand-New Day” in Los Angeles.

title: Paramount’s U.K. Concessions Give ‘Powerful Credibility’ to State AGs’ Lawsuit, Block the Merger Coalition Says: ‘The Dangers’ in U.S. Market ‘Are Unmistakable’
description: A coalition group campaigning against the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery has said the U.K.’s approval of the merge
body:
A coalition group campaigning against the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery has said the U.K.’s approval of the merger after obtaining “major concessions” lends “powerful credibility” to the pending legal case in the U.S.

	Earlier this week the U.K. confirmed the merger had received necessary approval to proceed after Paramount beefed up promises about programming ⁠and news provision in the country. These include not consolidating the group’s linear channels with on-demand services, ensuring Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network have distinct editorial staff and identities and maintaining Channel 5 News’ editorial independence.
	

	Following the concessions, the U.K.’s Competition and Markets Authority, media regulator Ofcom and secretary of state for culture, media and sport Lisa Nandy gave their approval to the merger.


	In the U.S, however, Paramount is facing an antitrust showdown against California attorney general Rob Bonta and a coalition of 11 other state AGs. The case is set to be heard next March.

	Block the Merger, which is made up of a number of groups opposing the $111 billion deal as well as celebrities such as Benedict Cumberbatch, said: “U.K. Secretary Nandy’s ability to obtain major concessions from Paramount lends powerful credibility to the case 12 state attorneys general have brought here in the U.S. If this merger required binding remedies even in the U.K., where Paramount and Warner hold a far weaker market position and the CMA has grown reluctant to block big mergers, the dangers in the more concentrated U.S. market are unmistakable. Here, the deal would unite two of the top three basic cable programmers and create exactly the anti-competitive, anti-consumer, and anti-creator harms our antitrust laws guard against.”

title: ‘PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie’ Review: The Dog-Cop Franchise Pushes an ACAB Message, Only It’s All Canines Are Benevolent
description: “PAW Patrol… are they still a thing?” asks Mayor Humdinger, the villain of “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie” — a rare moment of irony in a film otherwise
body:
“PAW Patrol… are they still a thing?” asks Mayor Humdinger, the villain of “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie” — a rare moment of irony in a film otherwise unfashionably devoid of it. That lack of second degree should by rights be charming, in a film landscape where fourth walls are constantly being torn to the ground, but that would be counting without the unsettlingly upbeat pups at the film’s centre, the scourge of parents to pre-schoolers around the world. That demographic will surely produce strong box-office takings for this new installment, which represents something of a step up in ambition for the franchise.
	

	A précis for the uninitiated may be in order before tending to the film itself: The PAW Patrol is a highly trained brigade of six/seven anthropomorphic puppies, each kitted out with colour-coded outfits, gadgets and a vehicle of their own, who go around solving problems and fighting crimes. Think Power Rangers done doggy-style.


	As the film begins, the relentlessly chipper puppies — including such apparently interchangeable characters as Chase (voiced by Rain Janjua), a German Shepherd who wears blue, or Rocky (William Desrosiers), a mixed breed who wears green — are patrolling the high seas with their ten-year-old handler Ryder (Henry Bolan), for reasons unexplained. Having put out a fire on board a yacht belonging to a family of TikTokers whom anybody else would have left to their fate, the dogs find themselves caught in a storm that sends them off course, towards an island where dinosaurs still roam free. 

	That would seem to be a drastic change of register for PAW Patrol, until you remember that there are toys to be sold. On the island, the team makes the acquaintance of Rex (Hayden Chamberlain), a paraplegic dog who has been stranded there for two years and in that time has befriended the dinosaurs and constructed an elaborate treehouse for himself. 
	

	Eagle-eyed viewers may spot that that last part is almost a wholesale rip-off of the 2023 animated feature “Kensuke’s Kingdom,” but surely won’t mind that some of that film’s grace appears to have rubbed off on this film’s animation and production design teams. The instigating seastorm is rendered in vivid detail, as is the diverse vegetation on the island, seized with finely differentiated grades of light and shadow. One sequence, in which firefighting Dalmatian Marshall (voiced by Carter Young, and taking on main character duties in this story) adventures into the jungle at night, even feels indebted to “Sleeping Beauty”-era Disney. 

	But these technical qualities only throw into relief the plastic, uncanny-valley feel of the characters whizzing about this latter-day Skull Island. As disquietingly big-eyed as any Margaret Keane subject, the pups have a horribly unreal veneer to them, like so many yassified Lassies with branded hard-hats and gleaming new trucks and jets in violent declensions of neon. Add to this a gratingly clipped vocal delivery from the kids voicing the puppies — no British child has sounded their T’s like that since the 1950s — and a bunch of “never give up” homilies in the screenplay, and you get a powerful recipe for animation kryptonite. 

	But worse is to come: the pups, having apparently stumbled upon heaven on earth, and being the incorrigible narcs they are, alert the authorities, leading to a chain of events that brings modernity and destruction to this prelapsarian paradise. Of course, the fault is nominally that of Mayor Humdinger (voiced with commendable relish by Ron Pardo), who, alerted to the island’s reserves of natural diamonds, takes accomplices and a truckload of dynamite to these shores in the hope of making a quick buck. 

	But the dogs started it. That the film can’t see this is a sign of how muddled its politics are, especially in its treatment of the tension between nature and modernity. Rex’s treehouse is full of lovely Rube Goldberg contraptions and, he boasts, doesn’t have wifi — but the film can’t leave him alone with his pre-industrial achievements, instead supplying him with shiny new gadgetry. Mayor Humdinger is depicted as venal, and is shown polluting the island with his rusted jalopy, but the dogs selling out their fellow animals to news stations are not considered morally wrong, and their cars and planes are cool because, presumably, they’re new. “PAW Patrol,” at heart, is skeptical of what is old and unheroic, and embraces a simplistic, macho, borderline libertarian worldview at odds with its environmentalism, altruism and artistry.
	

	Still, somehow, the film does eventually cohere into a half-decent entertainment, as Humdinger’s greed leads to an environmental disaster that threatens to destroy dogs and dinos alike. Some well-conceived action sequences, set against a backdrop of surprisingly apocalyptic volcanic activity, drum up a fair bit of jeopardy and suspense, and there is even a hint of something like character development for Marshall as he rises to the challenge of saving the day. 

	Parents are likely to be divided as to whether the fact that the film is aimed squarely at young people, with very little in the way of jokes for adults, is a good or a bad thing. Millennial and late Gen-Z viewers do get one freebie, though, in the form of “Bottle Up”, a new song written by Ed Sheeran for the Backstreet Boys. Those ‘boys’ are in their late forties and fifties now — a comforting reminder, to parents who may be despairing about enduring another entry in this franchise, that all children eventually grow up.

title: Natalie Portman, Jenna Ortega Satire ‘The Gallerist’ Lands at Roadside, Vertical
description: “The Gallerist,” a Miami-set satire of the art world starring Natalie Portman and Jenna Ortega, has been acquired by Roadside Attractions and Vertic
body:
“The Gallerist,” a Miami-set satire of the art world starring Natalie Portman and Jenna Ortega, has been acquired by Roadside Attractions and Vertical.

	The movie will open in theaters on Dec. 4, nearly a year after it premiered at Sundance Film Festival. 

	Cathy Yan directed “The Gallerist,” a dark comedic thriller in which Portman portrays an artist who is trying to make a name for herself at Art Basel in Miami and ends up trying to cover up a fatal accident by selling the dead body as a work of art. Sterling K. Brown, Zach Galifianakis, Da’Vine Joy Randolph and Catherine Zeta-Jones round out the cast.
	

	“Cathy Yan’s wildly original film was a winner for us at Sundance,” Roadside Attractions Co-Presidents Howard Cohen and Eric d’Arbeloff and Vertical CEO and Partner Peter Jarowey said. “She assembled a phenomenal ensemble cast led by Natalie Portman’s standout performance as a woman at the intersection of art and crime, revealing a dazzling comic edge along the way. It’s as fun as it is terrifying.”


	James Pedersen wrote the film, produced by Ash Sarohia, Sophie Mas and Portman, Jonathan King, Tom McCarthy, Rae Baron and Zola Elgart Glassman.

	Variety’s chief film critic Peter Debruge described “The Gallerist” as “facile but fun.” In his review, he wrote that “the intermittently clever movie is full of art-world in-jokes, but seems oblivious to its many plot holes.”

	Roadside’s upcoming releases include the Meghan Markle-produced doc “Cookie Queens” and horror film “Buddy,” featuring Cristin Milioti and Keegan-Michael Key. Vertical has “The Weight” starring Ethan Hawke and Russell Crowe, as well as “The Magic Faraway Tree” led by Andrew Garfield and Claire Foy.

title: ‘Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders’ Wraps From Little Spark Films; YA Mystery Follows Podcaster Hunting a Serial Killer (EXCLUSIVE)

	“Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders,” a YA mystery film from Little Spark Films, has wrapped filming in A
body:
A new gumshoe is on the case.

	“Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders,” a YA mystery film from Little Spark Films, has wrapped filming in Arlington, Texas. Mary Beth McAndrews directed the feature from a script by Preston Fassel, based on a concept by Cameron Hazelwood.

	Per a press release, the film is about “the eponymous 20-something sleuth, the hostess of a popular true crime podcast called ‘Hot Coffee, Cold Cases.’ For her latest case, Bridgette is dispatched to the remote East Texas town of Whisper Creek, where a long-dormant serial killer known as The Flower King has resurfaced. Haunted by memories from her own rural past, Bridgette must uncover the truth in a place where everyone is a suspect.”
	

	Newcomer Amanda Huerta, who was discovered in a Little Spark Film “48-Hour Spark” film race, leads the cast, which also includes Lisa Gaye (the “Toxic Avenger” franchise), Kelli Maroney (“Fast Times at Ridgemont High”), Alexandra Broussard and Larissa Dali (the “Becky” franchise).


	“While we were in pre-production, we also hosted a 48 Hour Film Race entitled ’48 Hour Sparks’ where our Office P.A.-turned-2nd-AD Jacob Harper had worked with Amanda,” Little Spark co-founder Catalina Querida said in a press release. “Seeing how quickly she was able to take on his 48 Hour film, ‘Music to my Ears,’ we thought she would fit the role as our confident hero.”

	When describing the film in its press release, Fassel said, “I had a few personal initiatives, including doing a YA story in the vein of what I grew up with — ‘Tuck Everlasting’, ‘Bridge to Terabithia’, ‘Maniac Magee’ — this non-IP, thoughtful approach that spoke to its audience as real people. Something that I’d show a theoretical daughter of mine, about a girl I imagine would be what that daughter would turn out like. And my hope is I’ve delivered a teen ‘Twin Peaks’ that mothers can use to introduce their daughters to David Lynch.” 
	

	“As a certified weird girl, now is the time for Weird Girl Cinema, and I couldn’t be more grateful to direct an entry into that growing pantheon,” McAndrews added in the release. “‘Bridgette Wrona’ is a film for all the weirdos out there who are passionate, creative, smart, and a little different from the world around them. My hope is that teens will watch this and feel inspired to dive further into the world of genre films; we don’t get a lot of true gateway horror anymore! This is gateway horror for the girls out there who spend their days watching true crime videos and reading about serial killers.”

	“Bridgette Wrona” was produced by Querida and Dali. Joe Manco and Chris Rushing served as executive producers. Fassel served as associate producer. Robert “Ghoulio” Alcala was the DP on the film.

	“Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders” is currently in post-production.

title: ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Power $239 Million U.K., Ireland July Box Office
description: Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey” topped the U.K. and Ireland box office in July with a gross of £56.2 million ($75.6 million), as the market posted
body:
Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey” topped the U.K. and Ireland box office in July with a gross of £56.2 million ($75.6 million), as the market posted a total of £178.2 million ($239.7 million) for the month, 35% ahead of the equivalent five-week period in July 2025, according to Rentrak.

	The 2025 comparison total of $177.1 million was driven by “Jurassic World Rebirth,” “Superman,” “The Fantastic Four: First Steps” and “F1 The Movie,” which contributed $44 million, $34 million, $23.7 million and $15.2 million respectively. Year-to-date U.K. grosses have passed $1.05 billion, running 18% ahead of 2025 and 34% ahead of 2024.
	

	After three weeks on release, “The Odyssey” is the highest-grossing title of 2026 so far, ahead of “Michael” ($71.4 million) and “Toy Story 5” ($71.6 million). Nolan’s action epic is now his fourth-highest-grossing film, closing in on “The Dark Knight Rises” ($76 million), “Dunkirk” ($76.4 million) and “Oppenheimer” ($80.4 million). The film opened to $16.7 million, the second-biggest opening of Nolan’s career behind “The Dark Knight Rises” ($19.2 million). At the same stage of release, “Oppenheimer,” “Dunkirk” and “The Dark Knight Rises” had grossed $57.3 million, $56.6 million and $59.2 million respectively, putting “The Odyssey” well ahead of pace and on track to become Nolan’s highest-grossing release.


	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” placed second with $71.3 million. Destin Daniel Cretton’s film opened to $49 million including previews, an opening bettered only by “Spectre” ($55.4 million) and “Avengers: Endgame” ($58.4 million), which went on to gross $128 million and $119.3 million respectively. “Brand New Day” is now the second-highest-grossing “Spider-Man” title behind “Spider-Man: No Way Home” ($130.9 million). After one week of release, “No Way Home” had grossed $62.4 million, meaning “Brand New Day” is tracking 14% ahead. Sony’s release joins “Star Wars: The Force Awakens,” “Spectre” and “Avengers: Endgame” as the only films to gross more than $67.3 million in their opening week, all three of which rank among the eight highest-grossing films of all time in the U.K.
	

	“Toy Story 5,” the top film in June, placed third for July after adding $28 million. The Pixar sequel is now the second-biggest title of the year, having overtaken “Project Hail Mary” ($46.5 million), “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” ($51.8 million) and “Michael” ($71.4 million), before being passed by “The Odyssey.” It is now the seventh-best-performing animated title in U.K. box office history, ahead of “Despicable Me 4” ($65.4 million) and behind “Frozen 2” ($72.2 million).

	“Minions & Monsters” followed at No. 4 with $20.8 million. Pierre Coffin’s third standalone “Minions” title opened to $5.8 million, a debut comparable to “Sonic the Hedgehog” ($6.3 million) and “Hoppers” ($6.5 million), which went on to gross $26.0 million and $19.0 million respectively. PostTrak exit polling gave the film a full five stars and a 91% Total Positive rating from kids, ahead of “Minions: The Rise of Gru,” which scored four stars.

	“Moana” rounded out the top five with $15.2 million. The live-action remake opened at a similar level to the 2016 animated original, debuting to $3.8 million versus the original’s $3 million opening en route to a $27.2 million lifetime gross. The new version also received a full five-star PostTrak rating across all audiences.

	Olivia Wilde’s “The Invite” took No. 6 with $4.8 million, her second-highest-grossing film behind “Don’t Worry Darling” ($14.1 million) and ahead of “Booksmart” ($2 million). Among comedies, it has grossed similarly to “The Phoenician Scheme” ($4.3 million) and “A Real Pain” ($4.8 million), and it is now Black Bear’s fifth-biggest release, ahead of “The Monkey” ($4.2 million) and behind “Ferrari” ($5.6 million).

	“Obsession” placed seventh for the third consecutive month, adding $3.2 million. Curry Barker’s film has climbed to third on the all-time U.K. horror chart, overtaking “The Conjuring: Last Rites” ($24.6 million) and “It: Chapter Two” ($25.4 million). Its cumulative gross of $26.2 million trails only “The Woman in Black” ($28.6 million) and “It” ($43.4 million), making it the highest-grossing horror release since 2017.

	“Evil Dead Burn” grossed $3.2 million at No. 8, the third-most-successful entry in the franchise, ahead of “Evil Dead II” ($1.6 million) and behind “Evil Dead” (2013) ($4.6 million). It ranks as the year’s fifth-highest-grossing horror title, ahead of “The Mummy” ($3.0 million) and “Ready or Not 2: Here I Come” ($2.8 million).
	

	“Supergirl” added $2.7 million at No. 9. Craig Gillespie’s DC Studios film is his second-biggest, behind “Cruella” ($12.8 million) and ahead of “I, Tonya” ($5.2 million). It overtook fellow DC Studios release “Blue Beetle” ($6.2 million) in July and is closing in on “Shazam! Fury of the Gods” ($8.1 million).

	“Disclosure Day” closed out the top 10 with $2 million for the month. Its $17.2 million lifetime gross now sits close to “Hook” ($16.9 million) and “Schindler’s List” ($19.2 million) in Steven Spielberg’s filmography.

	August opens with Eli Roth’s “Ice Cream Man” (Studiocanal), “Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie” (Paramount) and “Super Troopers 3” (Disney), all released Aug. 7. 

	The following week brings the Ewan McGregor and Anne Hathaway-led “The End of Oak Street” (Warner), New Zealand comedy “Holy Days” (Munro), family fantasy “Momo & the Time Thieves” (Signature) and “Sunny Dancer” (True Brit) on Aug. 14, alongside Matt Johnson’s Anthony Bourdain biopic “Tony” (A24), which expands wide on Aug. 21 alongside “Coyote vs. Acme” (Altitude), “David” (Vue/Angel), “Insidious: Out of the Further” (Sony), Jason Statham’s “Mutiny” (Studiocanal) and Black Bear comedy “Spa Weekend.” 

	The month closes on Aug. 28 with re-releases of “The Fast and the Furious” (Universal), “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” (Warner), “Kiki’s Delivery Service” (Anime Ltd) and “La La Land” (Lionsgate), plus new openers “Dog Stars” (Disney), “De Gaulle: Resistance” (Entertainment), “The Pout-Pout Fish” (Vertigo) and “One Night Only” (Universal).

title: New Radicals’ Gregg Alexander Soft-Relaunches Band With ‘One Night Only’ Movie Song Ahead of Their First Album in 28 Years
description: Gregg Alexander wasn’t planning to make a splashy return with New Radicals, his pop-rock collective that burned bright and fast in the late 1990s be
body:
Gregg Alexander wasn’t planning to make a splashy return with New Radicals, his pop-rock collective that burned bright and fast in the late 1990s before abruptly disbanding. So it’s fitting that “One Night Only (Break Loose Break Free!),” the group’s first new song in 28 years, arrived last Friday without warning. Its release was so under the radar, in fact, that it was a virtual obstacle course to track down the song on streaming services, unlisted on New Radicals’ own profile pages yet discovered and disseminated far and wide across the media.
	

	“It’s like most things that happen in New Radicals’ world: organically and seemingly out of nowhere,” Alexander tells Variety just days after its release. The jubilant tune, written and recorded as the title track for Will Gluck’s freshly released new rom-com “One Night Only,” picks up right where New Radicals left off, setting jaunty handclaps and candy-sweet melodies against heavier lyrics that question the systems humming just in the background of society. Alexander, who largely stays out of the limelight, met the song’s fervent reaction with typical candor: “Sometimes, you just hop on the roller coaster and go along for the ride.”


	For Alexander, that’s been something of a de facto mantra over the past three decades as New Radicals have endured well beyond their heyday. Since releasing their sole album “Maybe You’ve Been Brainwashed Too” in 1998, the set’s lead single “You Only Get What You Give” has become a song of the people, a cross-generational hit that rallies against corporate America with a sentiment that’s trickled down family trees. Last year alone, Geese went viral with a cover of the song on BBC Radio 1 Live Lounge; the MTV Video Music Awards featured a re-recorded version with Benee in a promo; and Journeys reimagined its iconic video set to a cover by Gus Dapperton.
	

	All of this, says Alexander, is partly what’s inspired him to revive New Radicals, a project he dismantled at the peak of its powers after getting a cold, hard look inside the star factory. But mostly, he says, it boils down to New Radicals’ ethos — how a song can potentially change the world. “I am intrigued by the idea of what would happen with a song as good as the best that I could do, if it went out there again,” he says during our three-hour interview. “And I do have some songs, I think, that are in that pantheon and can proudly stand next to ‘You Get What You Give.’ I am a true believer that if it’s meant to be to have a song reach the world the same way, then hopefully it will come to be.” (Watch a teaser for the “One Night Only” video below.)



	That’s largely been the driving force behind Alexander bringing back New Radicals, which has been slowly emerging from the shadows over the past few years. (I remind Alexander that when we first spoke in 2018, he said he had “seven to 10” New Radicals albums that he’d potentially release after he dies. He heartily laughs when I refer to the records as a “post-mortem.”)

	In the time since, the group has reawakened, however slowly. In 2021, Alexander teamed with band member Danielle Brisebois to perform “You Get What You Give” at President Joe Biden’s inauguration, and in 2024, they released New Radicals versions of Sophie Ellis-Bextor’s “Murder on the Dancefloor” and the Oscar-nominated “Lost Stars,” sung by Maroon 5’s Adam Levine for the 2014 film “Begin Again.” (Alexander wrote both songs, while Brisebois co-wrote the latter.) “Murder on the Dancefloor” had its own recent renaissance after its use in “Saltburn,” while Natasha Bedingfield’s “Unwritten” and “Pocketful of Sunshine,” both written by Brisebois, had similar resurgences.

	Now, New Radicals have had yet another revival, this time by their own hand. Just last month, they teamed with Michelle Branch to release a rerecording of her 2002 smash with Santana, “The Game of Love,” which Alexander initially wrote before filtering the demo through Tina Turner and Macy Gray. (A video for the duet with Branch is on the way.) And, after releasing “One Night Only,” New Radicals are officially returning to the stage they once shunned with plans to release their sophomore album “Maybe You’ve Been Brainwashed TWO (THE Heathen Will ‘CON$pirituality’ TROLL),” which is currently without a release date but in gestation.
	

	“It’s basically where we are right now between organized religion and politics and even social media,” explains Alexander about the record. He says that the “beautiful response” internally they got to “One Night Only” only fanned the flames of wanting to test the waters with more new music. “It seemed like a point of entry in the same way releasing the demo of ‘Murder on the Dancefloor’ or ‘Lost Stars’ was a way of just reminding ourselves what we do best, which is really just writing songs and singing. It’s easy to get lost with all of the different distractions about what our purpose is on this earth. It could be caretakers for those we love. It could be if there’s a cause that we believe in. It could be trying to be there as a support system if a friend is going through a depressing time. But at the core of who I am is a singer and a songwriter, and dare I say even occasionally an entertainer. It’s good to remind yourself why you were put on this earth. And I think music was the main reason.”



	

					(From L-R) Brandi Carlile, Cameron Crowe, Alexander, Roger Friedman, Dave Grohl. Courtesy of c2026Showbiz411.
	



	The announcement comes on the heels of Branch and New Radicals’ “The Game of Love,” originally a hallmark post-millennium tune that hit just a few years after Alexander called it quits on the industry as a front man. At the time, it was a ubiquitous smash, a song that Alexander performed only once after it was awarded song of the year at the 2004 BMI Pop Awards. Decades later, Branch asked Alexander to produce a new version of the track, potentially with Olivia Rodrigo in mind for a duet, before they concluded that his vocal was the right fit. After they cut the song, Alexander was on his way back from Prague to New York City to play it as a surprise for Clive Davis, who was involved in the song’s initial creation, when he learned that the music icon had passed away.

	“Very few people lived as fully as Clive did, a family man who traveled everywhere and was a champion of music and artist rights,” says Alexander. “The fact that we got to make this record and now that it’s going out there and getting a special response” — debuting on the Billboard Adult Pop Airplay chart last week — “we’re honored and touched because like anything I do, I always had zero expectations.”
	

	As much as Alexander has steered the New Radicals ship, “You Get What You Give” had also been coopted in ways they’d never imagined. One of the sticking points of their hit was its fast-paced riff against corporate America, bemoaning “big bankers buying” and “computers crashing down and cloning while they’re multiplying.” So it came as a surprise that an AI rendition of the song aired in a dramatic lead-in to the Super Bowl earlier this year, as well as in an AI rip-off that aired during an Olympic figure skater routine in February. Alexander addresses the usage by chalking it up to the indifference at a leadership level, and the impression it leaves on the masses.

	“The sad thing is I can’t speak to what will happen to all of people’s jobs being replaced, your voice being replaced, your songs being replaced. I feel like it’s so much bigger than that one usage,” he says. “But I do also feel that people feel disempowered because, do they really want to let their lives become consumed by it, or does somebody want to go just go write a better song? When are we going to wake up as the slow-boiling frog that we are and realize that if we don’t collectively demand that from an ethical and integrity and economic standpoint and in a survivability of our actual species standpoint, if we don’t collectively stand up to that, because it’s in all of our best interests, then we’re all fucked?”



	

					The back album cover of “Maybe You’ve Been Brainwashed TWO.” Courtesy of Bob Zuckerman.
	



	At present, Alexander is focused on the future of New Radicals and making sure music is at the center. He was recently credited as a songwriter on the Strokes’ “Going to Babble On,” included on the group’s new album “Reality Awaits” after he wrote the tune with Julian Casablancas five years ago. He’s planning on rolling out the video for “One Night Only,” a nod to a bygone era before cell phones when you could dance like no one’s watching. Most of all, he says, it’s about making music that resonates, however it may take hold.

	“The songs that you think are your best ones are the ones that often people don’t connect with,” he says. “And then something that you write as a throwaway, like ‘Murder on the Dancefloor’ or ‘You Get What You Give,’ are the ones that people remember out of my body of work. You have to be humbled by it and go, wow, I have to follow the lead of whatever connects with people. Because once you put a song out into the world or you write a book or you make a film, as soon as it goes out there, it’s really no longer yours. And so you have to just stand by and hopefully be proud of it if it gets a little bit of love from time to time.”

title: Selena Gomez, Christina Aguilera and Law Roach Board Olympics-Inspired Legacy House Host Committee (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Selena Gomez, Christina Aguilera, Law Roach, Ciara, Simu Liu and Jeff Goldblum are among those who have been named as founding honorary host committ
body:
Selena Gomez, Christina Aguilera, Law Roach, Ciara, Simu Liu and Jeff Goldblum are among those who have been named as founding honorary host committee members of the Olympics-inspired Legacy House in Los Angeles.

	Legacy House is a multi-year platform that will convene influential leaders through conversations, cultural events, partnerships and community initiatives designed to turn the momentum surrounding LA28 into lasting impact for Los Angeles. Legacy House will be open at a physical location in Culver City during the Olympics and Paralympics in 2028.
	

	Legacy House is led by Greg Propper, co-founder of A Day of Unreasonable Conversation, the annual summit that convenes leaders across entertainment, media, politics, business, sports and advocacy to foster constructive dialogue across differences. Propper, who is also a partner at business, politics and policy agency Bully Pulpit International, serves as Legacy House’s executive director.


	Programming will include moderated conversations, roundtables, podcasts, screenings, creator collaborations, working sessions, cultural gatherings, celebrations and partner-led activations exploring the intersection of sports, culture, philanthropy and civic impact.

	The honorary committee also includes Mike Amiri, Dustin Lance Black, Scott Budnick, Ciara, Tom Daley, Tara Davis-Woodhall, Rachel DeMita, Gabby Douglas, Julie Foudy, Ezra Frech, Myles Garrett, Emilie Goldblum, Ashlyn Harris, Gus Kenworthy, Michelle Kwan, John Legend, Dhar Mann, Nneka Ogwumike, Isaac Rochell, Tracee Ellis Ross, Matt Rutler, Jake Shane, Chrissy Teigen, Darren Walker, Abby Wambach, Koya Webb, Russell Westbrook, Russell Wilson and Hunter Woodhall.
	

	While not officially affiliated with LA28, Legacy House is in close communication with Olympic organizers. Operating as a 501(c)(3), the venture is nonpartisan, and is fiscally sponsored by the Social Impact Fund.

            James Harden's Texas gun case has been dismissed ... after the NBA star was arrested in Houston and charged with the unlawful carrying of a weapon.
      
    
            The Harris County District Attorney submitted the dismissal request Thursday -- which was obtained by TMZ -- after prosecutors say Harden completed an "alternative resolution agreement."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It's unclear what the agreement is ... but a judge signed off on the motion and dismissed the case on Thursday ... meaning the case won't be hanging over Harden's head by the time the NBA season rolls around in the fall.
      

            We broke the story ... Harden was arrested in Houston on June 13 after cops say he had a handgun in his vehicle during a traffic stop. Officers said the gun was in plain view and not being carried in a holster.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Harden was taken into custody, charged with a misdemeanor, and later released on bond.
      
    
            He has not publicly commented on the arrest or dismissal.
      
    
            Harden is currently a free agent, but he's expected to sign a multiyear contract to return to the Cleveland Cavaliers.

                          Postpones SF Show After 'Cardiac Incident' ...

                                                                        Published 
                              August 7, 2026

                                  August 7, 2026
                                9:08 AM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Earth, Wind & Fire hit the pause button on their Thursday night concert in San Francisco with Lionel Richie after one of their band members fell seriously ill.
      
    
            The legendary funk band posted a statement on Instagram, saying they were unable to perform at SF's Chase Center because of a medical emergency involving the band member, who was not identified.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The music group has changed throughout the years, but the notables are Maurice White, Verdine White, Philip Bailey, Myron McKinley and Ralph Johnson -- and went on to say the show would be rescheduled for a later date, which would be announced soon.
      

            The statement ended with, "We sincerely apologize for the unexpected change and appreciate everyone’s understanding." The band has since removed the statement, but a similar statement from the venue echoed the band's comments.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Mariano Elias, a rep for the SF Fire Department, tells TMZ ... a fire engine and a private ambulance responded Thursday night to the Chase Center for a "cardiac incident."
      
    
            Elias said the ambulance transported one person to a local hospital, where the patient was listed in critical condition. The patient's identity was not released due to HIPAA laws.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            You may recall ... on June 24, Lionel Ritchie also suffered a medical emergency while he was onstage in St. Paul, Minnesota.
      
    
            Richie cut his performance short at the Grand Casino Arena in St. Paul, Minnesota, after saying he felt "dizzy" and "strange" ... so much so, he actually took a seat on one of the stage platforms while singing "Dancing on the Ceiling." He postponed two shows before resuming the tour with Earth Wind & Fire in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, on June 30.
      
    
            We've reached out to reps for Earth Wind & Fire on the latest health scare ... they referred us to the band's IG statement.
